headlines.summary: Shares of CoreWeave sank 15%, while yields in its bonds blew out further.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave stock sinks as bond yields surge near 15% Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Shares of CoreWeave sank, while yields in its bonds surged higher. Elon Musk responded, "yikes" to the moves, pointed out on X by Chamath Palihapitiya late Tuesday. CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. Oracle shares also dropped. In this article CRWV ORCL NBIS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:39 02:39 CoreWeave falls amid AI debt fears Power Lunch CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out. Shares of the so-called neocloud nosedived 15.5%, while yields on its debt jumped higher. The yield to maturity on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 is sitting at 14.8%, while that of its 9.75% bond due in 2031 is around 14.9%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves in a memo obtained by CNBC. "When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations." While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said. "The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back." Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya , founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes." Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk." 'Relatively bad' balance sheet CoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained. "The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said. "It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running." CoreWeave, 1 month He expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November. CoreWeave's overall credit rating is a B+ at S&P Credit Ratings, which is junk bond territory. With rates in general having risen lately, it's natural that highly-leveraged companies, such as CoreWeave, are affected, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. CoreWeave "has capital expenditure levels that are almost hyperscaler-like, but it doesn't have the hyperscaler balance sheet," Nolan said. Tech sector hit CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares of Oracle closed down nearly 9% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%. The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite closing down 1.9%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest. Another neocloud stock, Nebius , dropped 10%. Dell cratered by roughly 11%. Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to surging supply of new bonds. For instance, hyperscalers Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle together have issued more than $228 billion in bonds, as of Oct. 14, according to LSEG. That is more than double the amount seen in all of 2025. All but Oracle have investment-grade ratings at S&P Credit Ratings. Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according to JPMorgan . By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said. — CNBC's Seema Mody contributed reporting. headlines.article_text: Dell stock plunges after Barclays downgrade on enterprise AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE, and NetApp on concerns that enterprise AI adoption is lagging. Dell tumbled 11%, leading the drop on Wall Street. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time," the Barclays analysts wrote. In this article NTAP DELL HPE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Technologies, speaking with CNBC at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 13th, 2026. CNBC Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout. Hewlett-Packard Enterprise , Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide. In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp , "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing." Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled. However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026. The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers. "There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time." The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%. In this article BAC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 5:33 05:33 Bank of America CEO on $1.2 billion fine: We're on the right course to remediate everything Squawk on the Street Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday. In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker . "We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said. The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April. They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said. Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time. In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI. Samuel Corum | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Department of Justice said Wednesday it is appealing a federal judge's decision to extend his order blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico. The notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit came less than a day after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the three outlets targeted by President Donald Trump can keep their access to the White House complex. That ruling, a preliminary injunction, replaces Kelly's temporary restraining order against the ban that Trump first announced on Sept. 18. It is not a final ruling in the ongoing lawsuit that the three news outlets filed against Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran and White House communications director Steven Cheung. Kelly, in an opinion filed Tuesday night, said the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claims that Trump and his co-defendants violated their First Amendment rights through unlawful retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. "It is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," wrote Kelly, whom Trump nominated in 2017 for his current seat. "In other words, it was 'an effort to suppress the speaker's activity due to disagreement with the speaker's view' ... rather than to vindicate any other purportedly 'compelling governmental interest,' ... including maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security," he wrote.
